quote: Garman agrees to indemnify Sparkling and hold it harmless from any and all losses, damages and expenses including without limitation, court costs, arbitration fees, penalties, fines, amounts paid in settlement of claims and reasonable legal fees and expenses of investigation (collectively the "Losses") which Sparkling or any of its respective officers or directors may incur due to a breach of this warranty.
rationale: Section 13 contains a Vendor-side IP indemnity: Garman warrants it owns or controls all rights necessary to grant the licence and free of liens, and indemnifies Sparkling (and its officers and directors) for all Losses, including settlement amounts and legal fees, arising from breach of that warranty, backed by the usual infringement remedies of procuring rights, procuring an equivalent element, or replacing/modifying the Work (p0091–p0093). Section 15 expressly carves breaches of Section 13 out of the liability limitation, so the indemnity is uncapped and better than the fallback's 3x-fees super-cap. No indemnity runs from Sparkling to Garman anywhere in the Agreement, so there is no one-sided or broad Customer indemnity to narrow. The clause therefore meets the fallback (and much of the preferred) position on its material terms. Noted but not flagged as deviations: no express duty to "defend" or allocate defence control, no refund remedy if the infringing element cannot be cured, the ten-calendar-day claim notice is tighter than we would prefer, and the non-IP heads (Vendor breach of law, Vendor-caused data breach, gross negligence/wilful misconduct) are absent from the preferred position.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have limited Garman's ownership statement to materials Garman provides, and added a confirmation that Sparkling retains all right, title and interest in its own data (including data converted under Section 4) and materials. As drafted, "all related materials, logos, and names provided pursuant to the terms of this Agreement" would sweep in our own data and branding, which our playbook does not permit; we are content for Garman to keep ownership of its Software, Documentation, Improvements and Modifications.

ops.newText: logos, and names provided by Garman pursuant to the terms of this Agreement. No title to the intellectual property in the Work is transferred to Sparkling by this Agreement. Sparkling is and remains the owner of all right, title and interest (including all intellectual property rights) in and to Sparkling's data (including all data converted pursuant to Section 4) and all materials, logos, names and other information provided by Sparkling, and nothing in this Agreement transfers or assigns any such right to Garman or creates any joint ownership.
ops.oldText: logos, and names provided pursuant to the terms of this Agreement. No title to the intellectual property in the Work is transferred to Sparkling by this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Limit Garman's IP ownership to Garman-provided materials and confirm Sparkling retains all rights in its own data and materials.

quote: Garman is the owner of all intellectual property rights in the Work (including any Improvements or Modifications thereto), including all related materials, logos, and names provided pursuant to the terms of this Agreement. No title to the intellectual property in the Work is transferred to Sparkling by this Agreement.
rationale: Section 13 is the only IP ownership provision. Garman retaining ownership of the Work (Software and Documentation) and of Improvements and Modifications to it is acceptable — that is vendor platform ownership, and Sparkling holds a perpetual licence while fees are paid (17(a)) plus a perpetual escrow licence to use and change the Codes on Garman default or discontinued support (16(b)), which sits at the rule's fallback for deliverables. The material failure is the unqualified sweep of "all related materials, logos, and names provided pursuant to the terms of this Agreement": that is not limited to Garman-provided items and on its face captures Sparkling's own materials, branding and the Sparkling data Garman converts under Section 4(b). There is no anywhere-in-the-document statement that Sparkling retains rights in its data (Section 14 treats data only as confidential information), so the walk-away risk of Customer IP/data passing to the Vendor is live. Redline limits the ownership sweep to Garman-provided materials and adds a Customer Data/materials ownership sentence with a no-joint-ownership confirmation; it does not disturb Garman's ownership of its Software.
ruleTitle: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 15 excludes indirect damages but sets no monetary cap, so both parties remain exposed to unlimited direct damages; our position is a mutual cap at the greater of 12 months' fees and USD 1,000,000. Indemnification, confidentiality (Sections 13 and 14), gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement sit outside the cap, and Sparkling's payment of fees due is not treated as damages. We can accept a straight 12 months' fees cap if the USD 1,000,000 floor is an issue.

ops.newText: Except for Excluded Claims, each party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of (a) the fees paid or payable by Sparkling under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim and (b) USD 1,000,000. "Excluded Claims" means a party's breach of its confidentiality, data protection or security obligations, its indemnification obligations, its gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, and its infringement of the other party's intellectual property rights, and Sparkling's obligation to pay fees due under this Agreement shall not be treated as damages for the purposes of this Section 15. The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14.
ops.oldText: The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14.

proposal.summary: Add a mutual aggregate liability cap (greater of 12 months' fees or USD 1,000,000) with uncapped Excluded Claims

quote: The exclusive remedy of either party in a claim against the other under this Agreement shall be the recovery of its direct damages. In no event shall either party be liable to the other for the recovery of any special, indirect or consequential damages even if the defendant party had been advised of the possibility of such damages including but not limited to lost profits, lost revenues, failure to realize expected savings, loss of data and loss of use.
rationale: Section 15 is the only liability-limiting provision in the Agreement (no "aggregate liability" language appears elsewhere; Section 13 is an IP ownership clause with no indemnity, and Section 11 merely requires payment of Fee Schedule fees). It gives a mutual exclusion of indirect/consequential damages and mutually carves out Sections 13 (IP) and 14 (confidentiality), but contains no monetary cap at all, so each party — including Sparkling — bears unlimited liability for direct damages. That fails the fallback, which requires a mutual cap of at least 12 months' fees. The redline inserts the preferred mutual cap (greater of 12 months' fees or USD 1,000,000) with uncapped Excluded Claims (indemnities, confidentiality/data protection/security, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud, IP infringement) and confirms fees due are not "damages"; the existing Sections 13/14 carve-out is preserved. A straight 12 months' fees cap is an acceptable fallback.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added a carve-out allowing us to assign to an affiliate or to a successor in a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets on notice, and made consent for other assignments subject to a reasonableness standard, since our playbook does not accept a blanket bar on customer assignment with no M&A carve-out. We have also confirmed Garman may not assign to one of our competitors; if helpful, we can instead make the successor carve-out fully mutual on written notice.

ops.newText: (d) Sparkling may assign this Agreement, without the consent of Garman, to an affiliate or to a successor in connection with a merger, acquisition, reorganization or sale of all or substantially all of its assets or business, upon written notice to Garman. Otherwise, neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed, and Garman may not in any event assign this Agreement to a competitor of Sparkling.
ops.oldText: (d) Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party.

ops.newText: (c) except as permitted by Section 20(d), not assign this Agreement or transfer
ops.oldText: (c) not assign this Agreement or transfer

proposal.summary: Add affiliate/successor assignment carve-out for Sparkling, a reasonableness standard on consent, and bar assignment by Garman to our competitors.

quote: (d) Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party.
rationale: Section 20(d) is a flat consent requirement on any assignment with no carve-out for an affiliate or a successor in a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets, and no reasonableness standard on consent — so it fails even the fallback (mutual right to assign to successors on written notice, consent otherwise not unreasonably withheld) and sits in walk-away territory as a blanket prohibition on customer assignment with no M&A carve-out. Section 3(c) compounds this by barring Sparkling from assigning or transferring except as Garman authorizes in writing. There is no change-of-control provision and no Garman termination or re-pricing right triggered by our change of control (Section 17 termination triggers are notice-based and insolvency-based only), so no deletion is needed there. Redline adds the affiliate/successor carve-out for Sparkling on notice, a not-unreasonably-withheld standard for other assignments, and a bar on Garman assigning to a competitor of ours; the Section 3(c) edit is a conforming cross-reference.

quote: Garman hereby grants to Sparkling, for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use: (i) the Software, safely in executable object code format, at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations; and (ii) the Documentation.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation on Sparkling, which meets the preferred position. The licence grant in § 2 is expressly non-exclusive; the restrictions in § 3 are ordinary software use/copying limits and do not prevent Sparkling from procuring competing software, maintenance or other services from third parties; § 10 (Maintenance and Support) and § 11 (Fees) contain no requirement that Sparkling take support or updates only from Garman; and the only other "exclusive" references (exclusive remedy in § 15, non-exclusive escrow licence in § 16, non-exclusive jurisdiction in § 20(h)) are unrelated to exclusive dealing. Nothing restricts our freedom to buy from other suppliers, so no redline is needed.

quote: Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman. If Sparkling terminates this Agreement pursuant to this Section 17(b), Sparkling shall cease using the Software at the end of the ninety (90) day notice period
rationale: The Agreement imposes no liquidated damages, penalty, cancellation charge or minimum/early-termination fee on Sparkling. Section 11 obliges Sparkling only to pay the fees set out in the Fee Schedule, and Section 17(b) gives Sparkling an unqualified right to terminate for convenience on 90 days' notice with no termination payment or stipulated damages. Section 15 confines each party's remedy to direct damages and excludes indirect/consequential damages, and there is no interest-on-late-payment or stipulated-damages mechanic. Where the Agreement does address termination for Garman's default (p0128), the money flows to us (fee refund and conversion to a perpetual royalty-free licence), which is favourable and not flagged. This meets the preferred position — no liquidated damages or penalties payable by the Customer — so no redline is proposed.
ruleTitle: Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added contractors acting on our behalf to the licensed user group (our affiliates are already covered) and a consent-free assignment right to a successor in a merger or sale of the business, consistent with our playbook position that the licence must reach our affiliates and contractors and follow us through an M&A transaction. Happy to make the successor carve-out mutual as drafted and to keep contractors bound by the Section 3 use restrictions.

ops.newText: for the use of Sparkling, affiliated companies of Sparkling and contractors acting on Sparkling's behalf, in each case operating at Authorized Locations
ops.oldText: for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations

ops.newText: (d) Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party, except that, notwithstanding Sections 2 and 3(c), either party may assign this Agreement and the licence granted hereunder, without consent, to a successor in connection with a merger, acquisition, reorganization or sale of all or substantially all of its assets or of the business to which this Agreement relates.
ops.oldText: (d) Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party.

proposal.summary: Extend licence to Sparkling's contractors and permit assignment of the licence to a successor in an M&A transaction.

quote: Garman hereby grants to Sparkling, for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use: (i) the Software, safely in executable object code format, at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations; and (ii) the Documentation.
rationale: The grant is good on two of the three material terms: our affiliates are expressly covered without any notice condition (better than the fallback), and the licence is perpetual so long as fees are paid (Section 17(a)) with no right for Garman to revoke at will — termination is limited to insolvency events and uncured material breach on 30 days' notice (Section 17(c)(7)), and on Garman's default the licence converts to a fully paid perpetual licence (p0128, p0115). It fails the fallback on transferability: the licence is "non-transferable", Section 3(c) bars assignment or sublicence to any Person absent Garman's written consent, and Section 20(d) requires the other party's consent for any assignment, with no successor/M&A carve-out. Contractors acting on our behalf are also unaddressed, so their use depends on Garman's discretionary consent. Redline adds contractors to the licensed user group and a consent-free assignment to a successor in a merger or sale of the business, reaching the preferred position with minimal change.

The agreement contains no non-compete or field-of-use covenant binding Sparkling, which meets the preferred position (no restriction on the businesses we operate or the products we buy or build). Section 3 ("RESTRICTIONS ON USE") is limited to conventional licence-scope restrictions on the Software and Documentation — no copying, no reverse engineering, no assignment or sublicence, and "not use the Work except as authorized herein" — none of which limits our freedom to acquire, develop or use competing routing software. Section 19 is a mutual one-year non-solicitation of employees (a separate category, and reciprocal rather than one-sided against us), and Section 20 and the confidentiality provisions in Section 14 impose no restrictive covenant; Section 14(c) in fact preserves independent development as a carve-out. Searches for "compet", "develop", "exclusiv", field-of-use and territory language returned no restriction on our business. No redline required.

quote: (b) Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman.
rationale: Section 17(b) gives us (Sparkling) an unconditional right to terminate at any time on 90 calendar days' written notice, with no early-termination fee or penalty, and Section 11/the Fee Schedule impose no accelerated payment on exit. Garman has no termination-for-convenience right anywhere: Section 17(c) permits termination only for insolvency events or uncured material default, and Section 17(a) makes the licence perpetual while fees are paid. That sits at the playbook fallback (customer notice of 60–90 days, no fee, no vendor convenience right) rather than the preferred 30 days, so it is acceptable and not redlined. Sub-elements short of preferred, noted only: the clause is silent on a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees on a convenience termination (a refund of fees for services not rendered applies only on termination for Garman's default under p0128, and full repayment on rejection under Section 8), and maintenance runs in renewable one-year terms, so any prepaid maintenance for the post-termination period would need to be recovered by agreement.

No audit, inspection or verification right binding Sparkling exists anywhere in the Agreement. Searches for "audit", "inspect", "verify", "records", "premises" and "access" return nothing that gives Garman any right to audit our use of the Software; the use restrictions in § 3 (p0029–p0037) impose only self-executing covenants with no accompanying inspection mechanic, and § 20 General Matters contains no audit provision. The only examination right in the document (p0114, escrow materials: "Sparkling may itself or by retaining independent experts, examine and test the materials for compliance with the obligations of Garman hereunder") runs in our favour. The complete absence of any Garman audit right is better than the playbook's preferred position (once per 12 months, 30 days' notice, independent auditor, Vendor's cost, no system access), and no remote or unannounced access to our systems is granted, so there is no walk-away exposure. We therefore raise nothing and deliberately do not introduce audit language, since inserting a limited audit right would create a vendor entitlement we do not currently have.

quote: (h) This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia. All disputes under this Agreement shall be subject to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Nova Scotia.
rationale: Section 20(h) is the only governing-law/venue provision (no arbitration clause appears anywhere; the sole reference to "arbitration fees" in the IP indemnity at p0090 is a costs reference only). The chosen law — Nova Scotia and the federal laws of Canada applicable there — is outside the playbook's accepted list (New York preferred; Delaware, California, or England and Wales as fallback), so on a literal parametric reading it fails the fallback. I am not treating this as a deviation to be redlined, however, because the clause runs in our favour and is nowhere near walk-away territory: Nova Scotia is our own home jurisdiction (Sparkling is at 19 Fielding Avenue, Dartmouth, NS per p0139), whereas the vendor is based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan (p0138). The clause therefore gives us home-forum law and courts rather than the vendor's home jurisdiction, the venue grant is non-exclusive (preserving our ability to sue elsewhere, e.g. where the vendor's assets sit), and there is no mandatory arbitration and no foreign seat. Moving this to New York would strip our client of its home-court advantage and add cost and foreign-law risk, so the playbook's direction rule ("do not flag a clause that benefits our party") governs over the accepted-jurisdiction list here. Flagging for business confirmation only: if the deal team specifically wants a US-law contract for portfolio consistency, the minimal edit is to swap "Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia" for New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County, leaving the rest of 20(h) intact. Absent that instruction, we recommend accepting 20(h) as drafted.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: Searches for MFN-type language ("most favoured nation", "no less favourable", "favourable/favorable", "best", "price", "other customers", "third part") return nothing resembling a pricing-parity or best-terms undertaking. The fees clause (§ 11) simply requires payment per the Fee Schedule, and § 20 (General Matters) contains only time-of-essence and notice provisions. There is accordingly no obligation on Sparkling (as Customer) to offer Garman terms no less favourable than those given to third parties or to match third-party offers, which matches the preferred position of no MFN burdening the Customer. No Vendor-granted MFN exists in our favour either, but that is a commercial upside we are not required to flag under this rule.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay obligation, shortfall charge or volume cap on Sparkling. Fees are payable only for the licence granted and services actually ordered: Section 11 simply requires payment of the Fee Schedule fees; Section 2 charges additional fees only if Sparkling elects to use the Software beyond the Authorized Locations; and maintenance under Section 10 runs on a "renewable one-year term" rather than a multi-year committed term. Sparkling also retains an unconditional right to terminate on ninety (90) days' notice (Section 17(b)), so there is no locked-in spend. Searches for "minimum", "commit", "take or pay", "shortfall", "volume" and "non-refundable" returned no customer-side commitment language. This meets the preferred position (no minimum commitment; fees for usage or ordered services only), so no redline is warranted.
ruleTitle: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept a no-hire covering all of the other party's employees, so we have narrowed this to a mutual non-solicitation limited to personnel directly involved in the services for 12 months after their involvement ends, with the usual carve-outs for general advertising and unsolicited approaches. This keeps the protection mutual while removing the restriction on ordinary hiring.

ops.newText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of twelve (12) months after the end of an individual's involvement in the provision of services under this Agreement, neither party shall directly solicit for employment any employee of the other party who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement. This restriction does not apply to, and neither party shall be restricted from hiring, any individual who (a) responds to a general advertisement or recruitment campaign not specifically targeted at the other party's personnel, or (b) approaches a party on his or her own initiative without any prior solicitation.
ops.oldText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Convert mutual no-hire into a narrow 12-month mutual non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved, with general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs.

quote: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.
rationale: Section 19 is a no-hire, not a non-solicit: it prohibits us (and our affiliates) from hiring "any employee of the other party" during the term plus one year, without limiting the first limb to personnel involved in the services and with no carve-out for general advertisements or unsolicited approaches. No-hire provisions covering all Vendor personnel sit in walk-away territory under this rule, so the clause fails the fallback on material terms. The redline converts it to a mutual non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved in the services, running 12 months from the end of their involvement, with general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs, consistent with the fallback and with the existing mutual bargain.

quote: For a renewable one-year term commencing upon the Maintenance Commencement Date, subject to payment of maintenance fees in accordance with the Fee Schedule but without additional fees or charges, Garman shall provide the following Maintenance Services:
rationale: The only renewing element is maintenance, which runs for "a renewable one-year term" (p0065) — a 12-month term that is renewable rather than automatically renewing, so renewal effectively requires the parties' agreement and there is no non-renewal notice window imposed on us and no multi-year auto-renewal. The licence itself is perpetual while fees are paid (p0117) and we may exit on 90 days' notice at any time (p0118). This meets the preferred position (renewal by agreement, 12-month term, no opt-out hurdle) and is well clear of the walk-away triggers. Two preferred sub-elements are absent but immaterial and not redlined: there is no Garman renewal reminder and no express cap on maintenance fee uplift on renewal (fees are simply "in accordance with the Fee Schedule"); if the Fee Schedule permits Garman to reset renewal fees, we would ask commercially for a CPI/3% cap. We would also be content to clarify "renewable" as "renewable by mutual written agreement" as a drafting nit only.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 17 only requires Sparkling to return Garman's Software and Codes on termination; nothing obliges Garman to help us wind down or to give back our own data. We have added a new Section 17(d) providing up to six months of transition assistance at Garman's then-current rates, return of Sparkling's data in a machine-readable format within 30 days, and certified deletion thereafter. If six months is too long, we can accept 90 days of assistance with the same 30-day data export.

ops.text: (d) Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Garman shall (i) at Sparkling's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Garman's then-current rates; (ii) within thirty (30) calendar days of Sparkling's request, return to Sparkling all of Sparkling's data in Garman's possession or control in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (iii) thereafter delete such data from its systems and certify such deletion to Sparkling in writing.

proposal.summary: Insert transition assistance and Sparkling data return/deletion obligations on termination in Section 17

quote: (b) Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman. If Sparkling terminates this Agreement pursuant to this Section 17(b), Sparkling shall cease using the Software at the end of the ninety (90) day notice period, and shall certify to Garman within thirty (30) calendar days of termination that Sparkling has destroyed or has returned to Garman all Software, Documentation and Codes.
rationale: Section 17 addresses termination only one way: Sparkling must cease use and return or destroy Garman's Software, Documentation and Codes. There is no obligation on Garman to provide any wind-down or transition assistance, and no obligation to return Sparkling's data (which Garman handles under the Section 4 data conversion work) or to certify deletion. Section 8 return-of-Confidential-Information applies only if the reject option is exercised, and Section 18 survival adds nothing on exit assistance; searches for "transition" and "return" confirm no equivalent clause elsewhere. The agreement therefore fails even the fallback (90 days' assistance plus 30-day data export), so we insert a new Section 17(d) at the preferred position (six months' assistance at then-current rates, 30-day machine-readable data return, certified deletion thereafter), flagging the 90-day fallback in the comment.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return

quote: For the acceptance period and for a period of one year from the Maintenance Commencement Date, and thereafter for as long as the Software is covered by Maintenance Services and is used by Sparkling in accordance with this Agreement, Garman warrants that the Software shall perform in conformance with the Specifications in all material respects.
rationale: Section 12 gives an express conformance-to-Specifications warranty for the acceptance period plus one year from the Maintenance Commencement Date, and continuing for as long as the Software remains under Maintenance Services — at or beyond the preferred 12-month software warranty. Real remedies are provided: correction during acceptance testing (§6(b)), best-efforts repair at no charge under Software Repair Service (p0077), and, on rejection, return of all amounts paid to Garman (§7–§8). There is no "AS IS" language and no disclaimer of implied or other warranties anywhere in the Agreement, so nothing swallows the express warranty, and the §15 liability cap preserves direct damages. Minor preferred sub-elements are absent (no express professional-and-workmanlike services warranty, no compliance-with-laws or no-malicious-code warranty, and Software Repair Service is qualified by best efforts and chargeable-cause carve-outs); we note these but they do not defeat the fallback, so no redline.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added a short insurance provision, as the Agreement currently contains none even though Garman's personnel attend our sites for installation and training and convert our data. The limits reflect our standard position (CGL USD 1M/2M, E&O USD 2M, cyber USD 5M, certificates on request); if helpful we can work from E&O USD 1M and cyber USD 2M.

ops.text: (k) Garman shall maintain, at its own expense, throughout the term of this Agreement and for one (1) year thereafter: commercial general liability insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate; professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000; and, where Garman processes, converts, hosts or otherwise has access to Sparkling's data, cyber and privacy liability insurance of not less than USD 5,000,000. Garman shall also maintain workers' compensation insurance as required by applicable law. Garman shall provide Sparkling with certificates of insurance evidencing such coverage on request.

proposal.summary: Insert vendor insurance covenant (CGL, E&O, cyber, workers' comp) into General Matters.

quote: (i) All paragraph headings contained in this Agreement are for convenience only and shall not affect the interpretation of this Agreement.
rationale: A text search for "insurance" returns no results, and the General Matters section (p0134-p0136, p0141-p0147, p0149) runs from time-of-essence through entire agreement with no insurance covenant. Garman is a services-touching vendor: it installs the Software at Authorized Locations and converts Sparkling's data (p0041-p0042), and delivers on-site training and implementation support (sec-5, sec-9). With no coverage at all for a vendor that accesses our data and attends our premises, this falls below even the fallback (E&O USD 1M / cyber USD 2M) and into walk-away territory, so we insert a short insurance paragraph at the preferred limits as new clause 20(k), with workers' compensation and certificates on request. The fallback limits are offered in the comment.
